Reflection

I am someone who has been trying my best to avoid coding at all costs for a major portion of my life. I am nervous to jump in the deep end of using R, but also excited about learning about the course material, especially creating prediction models.

title: About Me
text: My name is Yogi Patnaik and I am a Master of Urban Spatial Analytics student at the University of Pennsylvania. I completed my Bachelor’s degree in geographic information science (GIS) from Arizona State University. I have been fond of maps and how much information they hold since I was young. This inspired me to look into what more I could accomplish using that location data, which led me into becoming a GIS student. As a MUSA student, I wish to be even more creative with how I can analyze location data and be better able to use the various tools that are used in the realm of the urban spatial analytics program. My topics of interest when it comes to the spatial world is the design of better roadways and the creation of better urban sustainability patterns and sustainable transportation networks.

title: Home
text:
Welcome to my portfolio for MUSA 5080: Public Policy Analytics at the University of Pennsylvania.
This site documents my work in the Master of Urban Spatial Analytics program — weekly notes, course assignments, and a final project applying data analysis to urban policy questions.


I’m a student in the MUSA program at Penn. My background is in GIS, and I’m interested in sustainability and transportation. I enjoy using spatial data to better understand how cities function and how people interact with the built environment. I’m particularly interested in how GIS and data analysis can help address transportation and environmental challenges. Through the MUSA program, I hope to strengthen my technical and analytical skills while applying them to real-world urban issues. Ultimately, I’d like to use these skills to help make cities more sustainable, accessible, and efficient.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
result <- filter(counties, population>50000) #keep the big ones!
“result” is the object
“<-” is an assignment arrow
“filter” is the function name (a verb)
“counties” is the input data
“population >50000” is the argument
install.packages(“packagename”)
library(“packagename”)
filter() – this picks rows. r in filter is for r as in rows
select() – this picks columns. c in select is for c as in columns
mutate() – adding a new computed column
new <- mutate(counties, income2)
arrange()– change order of rows i.e. asc, desc
group_by() + –> many rows become few
summarize()
columns, variables data frame = tibble (nicer, prints prettier)
step 1 <- filter (counties, moe_pct > 10)
step 2 <- arrange (desc(moe_pct))
step 3<- select(NAME, moe_pct))
that’s what a novice does,


“and then”
%>% or |>
new_data <- counties %>% filter(moe_pct>10)%>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))%>% select(NAME, moe_pct))%>%
The pipe is basically saying from counties do this and then this and then this (the result is passed down) and saving it to the data frame in one smooth function, instead of having the 3 steps listed above.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)

In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in California and compare how reliable the estimates are. I use the margin of error to identify which counties have more or less uncertainty in their rent estimates.

vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5")
View(vars)

my_state <- "CA"       
my_variable <- "B25064_001"    

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)


dim(county_data)

[1] 58  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California   B25064_001     2318    17
2 06003 Alpine County, California    B25064_001       NA    NA
3 06005 Amador County, California    B25064_001     1380   106
4 06007 Butte County, California     B25064_001     1369    31
5 06009 Calaveras County, California B25064_001     1615   142
6 06011 Colusa County, California    B25064_001     1139    67


The state of California has 58 counties, and the row count was also 58.


county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Sierra County, California        1181   705   59.7 
 2 Trinity County, California        922   220   23.9 
 3 Plumas County, California        1034   148   14.3 
 4 Mono County, California          1593   212   13.3 
 5 Mariposa County, California      1268   165   13.0 
 6 Calaveras County, California     1615   142    8.79
 7 Modoc County, California          818    71    8.68
 8 Lake County, California          1292   110    8.51
 9 Tuolumne County, California      1247   103    8.26
10 Inyo County, California          1140    88    7.72


Sierra County had the largest margin of error relative to the estimate, with a margin of error percentage of 59.7%.

Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    39
2 Low confidence      6
3 Moderate           13


[How many counties fall into each category?] From the total 58 counties in California, 39 counties were classified as high confidence, 13 as moderate confidence, and 6 as low confidence. —

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California     2318     17 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California        NA     NA    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      1380    106   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       1369     31  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   1615    142   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      1139     67   21895    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))


county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         39        989118.
2 Low confidence           6         11691.
3 Moderate                13         45926.


** [What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]**
The average population of high confidence counties is 989,117.82, and the average population of low confidence is 11,691.33. The pattern shows that less reliable estimates tend to occur in counties that have smaller populations.

We know the least about the smaller counties in California. Sierra County had a highest margin of error relative to its median gross rent estimate at 59.7%, and other smaller counties, like Trinity County, Plumas County, Mariposa County, and Mono County, had very high margins of error. These six counties, which were classified as low confidence had an average county population of 11,691.
Since the ACS only uses a sample of households rather than surveying every household in the country, there is less samples and therefore more uncertainty and larger margins of error when collecting data. The smaller counties having less reliable median gross rent estimates is explained by this.
This uncertainty plays a part in a situation where housing funding may be allocated based on an equally certain approach from a state agency. The high margins of error means that these smaller communities may be subjected to either too much money or too little money. Since the government has limited funding, a county receiving too much money can be detrimental to other counties who may need it. This ties into a county receiving too little money, because since their margin of error is not accounted for, the misallocation of funds further spirals.

The high margins of error means that these smaller communities may be subjected to either too much money or too little money. Since the government has limited funding, a county receiving too much money can be detrimental to other counties who may need it. This ties into a county receiving too little money, because since their margin of error is not accounted for, the misallocation of funds further spirals.

title: Week 3: GGPlot Basics
text:
The Ansombe’s Quartet is a set of 4 different appearing plots that have the same mean x and y, the same regression line, and the same correlation factor.
Plot is a mapping from columns in your data to visual properties on your page. (“Grammar of Graphics”) aka gg like from ggplot.



Your Data
Page (Canvas)




estimate
→ position on y-axis


population
→ position on x-axis



p <- 1. ggplot(the data you’re using) —> creates a blank canvas
aes(…) Aesthetic Mappings.
geom_*(…) the shape/type of chart e.g.
ggplot(tract_data) +
aes(x= population, y = moe_pct) +
geom_point()
ggplot(county_data) +
aes(x=estimate,y=population)+
geom_point(color=“blue”)



inside aes()
not inside




aes(color=reliability)
geom_point(“blue”) - decorations






What I want to know
GEOM




How a variable is spread?
geom_histogram()


How do two variables relate?
geom_point()


How do groups compare?
geom_boxplot()


How do things change over time?
geom_line()


How uncertain is a value?
geom_errorbar()



LOW: / MED: __ HIGH: ///
Coefficient of Variation (CV) - Relative measure of sampling error - Standard error / estimate * 100 - SE: 90%, MOE: 1.645 - 10,000 - Low CV 15% – high reliability Medium- 15-30% High- 30% High sampling error


Poverty Rate = # in Poverty MOE / Total Population MOE moe_sum()-> adding estimates together moe_prop()-> one estimate as share of another moe_ratio()-> Poverty / Income One not a subset of another
Change over time The overlapping intervals e.g. 2019-2023, 2018-2022
We need to compare non-overlapping intervals
e.g. \(2014-2018 45000 \pm 8,000\)
\(2019-2023 62000 \pm 11,000\)
MOE = 17,000?



\(SEdiff = \sqrt{SE_1 ^2 + SE_2^2}\)
\(z = (est_1 - est_2) / SEdiff\)
Confidence Interval of Change
\(difference \pm(1.645*SEdiff)\)

title: Week 4: Using Spatial Data in R
text:
Table Join
left_join(income_23, income_15, by=“GEOID”)
GEOID is the field where the tables join
income_23 and income_15 represent the median income in 2023 and 2015, and they are joined side by side
left_join = match everything to the field on the left, if not matching on right return NA
inner_join = match both tables
full_join = match every row, if not possible return NA
geometry -> “Sticky”, it sticks to the data
.shp = shapefile
.gdb = geodatabase
SF = sample features
Coordinate Reference Systems



Geographic
Projected




units: degrees
-



The Earth is a geoid which is irregular
We measure the Earth as an ellipsoid, and its axes.
It’s a good fit for some places and poor fit for others, because it cannot perfectly match the geoid.
NAD 27 - North American Datum - uses the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and uses Meades Ranch, Kansas as its datum/reference point
NAD 83 - uses the Earth centered GRS-80 ellipsoid - lines of latitude and longitude are different than NAD 27
WGS84 - Another Earth centered ellipsoid (This is the GPS standard)
